X-rays were discovered in Germany..why: People say who discovered X-rays and what he did in his laboratory, but hardly anyone states the country of the discovery itself. The direct form is rare (six hits for "discovered X-rays in Germany"), while the discoverer is named hundreds of times.

X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Röntge.why: Stated everywhere that X-rays are introduced.

Wilhelm Röntgen worked in Germany..why: Röntgen is tied to the University of Würzburg, in Germany, wherever his discovery is told; the exact phrase "worked in Germany" is not how it is written.

A discovery is made in the country where.why: True by what the words mean: a discovery made by someone who works in a country is made in that country.

The scientist who discovered X-rays work.why: Nobody writes where "the scientist who discovered X-rays" worked: people name Röntgen and his university, and the model joins them. The direct form is rare; the premises are common.

The main language of the country where X.why: The language of the country where something was discovered is not something anyone writes; the model resolves the country first and then its language. The direct form is rare.

X-rays and radioactivity were not discov.why: Texts give the discoverer and the year of each discovery, and the two are compared by year, not by country; the negative about the country is not stated. The direct form is rare.

X-rays were discovered in Würzburg..why: Wikipedia's Röntgen article says outright that Würzburg is where he discovered X-rays and that his laboratory there is kept as a memorial site.

sources.quote: In Würzburg, where Röntgen discovered X-rays, a non-profit organization maintains his laboratory and provides guided tours to the Röntgen Memorial Site.

In 1895, in his laboratory at the Physical Institute of the University of Würzburg, Röntgen was investigating the external effects of passing an electric discharge through various types of vacuum tube equipment

notes: A derived edit (very_likely): X-rays' country of discovery is worked out from the discoverer and where he worked. Replaces the earlier 'likely' supernova edit, which no model held. Premises: Röntgen discovered X-rays (stored), Röntgen worked in Germany (stored), and the definitional rule that a discovery is made where its discoverer worked. Worlds: the discovery goes to someone who worked in France (w1) or Röntgen moves to France (w2). The premise-route query asks where the discoverer worked: it is France in both worlds. Several exact phrases the stored claims need could not be counted before the infini-gram API refused further requests (see the build report); the Würzburg-based claims rest on approximate co-occurrence counts.
